name: Deficit Inverted Row
description: The deficit inverted row elevates the feet above the bar height so the body is declined rather than horizontal, dramatically increasing the percentage of bodyweight lifted compared to standard inverted rows. It effectively bridges the gap between bodyweight rows and full pull-ups, loading the lats and upper back with near-vertical force angles from a horizontal plane.

execution.starting_position: Place feet on a bench, box, or elevated surface above the bar. Grip the bar with an overhand or neutral grip. Body hangs below bar level, arms extended.
execution.setup_instructions: The greater the foot elevation, the more vertical the angle and the harder the exercise. Start with feet at the same height as the bar and progress to elevated positions.
steps: Step 1: Begin hanging below the bar with feet elevated, arms fully extended.
Step 2: Depress and retract scapulae to initiate.
Step 3: Row the chest to the bar by driving elbows back.
Step 4: At the top, chest should contact or nearly contact the bar.
Step 5: Lower under control to full arm extension.
execution.breathing_instructions: Exhale on the row. Inhale descending.
common_mistakes: Hips dropping below the torso line
Using excessive shoulder elevation instead of lat drive
safety_considerations: Ensure the elevated surface for feet is stable and won't slide
Use a sturdy rack or bar rated for bodyweight suspension
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Full arm extension to chest at bar level.
coaching_cues: The more you elevate the feet, the harder it gets
Body stays rigid — no hip drop
